I want to aggregate V5 over common rows sequentially as follows:

a       b       d       g       20

a       c       e       h       5
a       c       e       g       10
a       c       e       h       10
a       c       f       g       10

where seqAggregate.data.frame is aggregate.data.frame with the following lines

FUN=sum)[,-5]

>> aggregate(VZ.df$V5, by=VZ.df[,c("V1","V2","V3","V4","jj")],
>> FUN=sum)[,-5]
>>

>> to a minute-by-minute dataframe of 5 columns and 1440 rows.
>> However, when I applied it to my actual data frame which is
>> 5 columns and 17280 rows (corresponding to a row every 5
>> seconds of a day) I got an error message that the object
>> size was 5.8E6, exceeding the default of 5E6.  So, I set
>> options(object.size = 5E7) and ran the function again.
>> This hung up my computer (400 MHz 12 GB PC) both times I
>> tried it, so I'm wondering how I can free up memory or make
>> the program more efficient from a memory standpoint.
>> Any suggestions?   Also, would Solution B be more memory
>> efficient?

No! It's as unefficient as Solution A for large data frames.

The 'problem' in both solutions is aggregate.data.frame
or more precisely the call
aggregate(VZ.df$V5, by=VZ.df[,c("V1","V2","V3","V4","jj")], ...)
with a large data frame VZ.df[,c("V1","V2","V3","V4","jj")].

Actually only the last column in VZ.df is needed to aggregate
V5 over common rows.

A more efficient solution is therefore:

groupSeq <- function(by){
  x <- codes(interaction(by))
  ends <- c(diff(x)!=0, T)
  pos <- seq(along=x)[ends]
  len <- diff(c(0, pos))
  list(ID=rep(seq(along=len), len), pos=pos)
}

agg <- function(x, by, FUN=sum, ...){
  g <- groupSeq(by)
  x <- tapply(x, g$ID, FUN=FUN, ...)
  data.frame(by[g$pos,], x)
}

## Example 1 (small)
VZ.df <- data.frame(V1=rep("a",12),
                    V2=c(rep("b",4),rep("c",8)),
                    V3=c(rep("d",4),rep("e",6),rep("f",2)),
                    V4=c(rep("g",5),"h","g","g","h","h","g","g"),
                    V5=rep(5,12))

agg(VZ.df$V5, VZ.df[,1:4])
   V1 V2 V3 V4  x 
 4  a  b  d  g 20
 5  a  c  e  g  5
 6  a  c  e  h  5
 8  a  c  e  g 10
10  a  c  e  h 10
12  a  c  f  g 10

## Example 2 (large)
N <- 20000
X <- data.frame(matrix(sample(letters[1:8], size=N*4, replace=T),
                       ncol=4), X5=rep(5,N))
res <- agg(X$X5, X[,1:4])

Of course, you can also use Bill Dunlap's approach in function
groupSeq (i.e. a combination of 'do.call("paste", ...' and 'rle')
which might be more efficient than 'interaction' 
(but probably not that elegant).

-- Christian Keller

messages.body_plain:
Last week I asked (in a two part question) how to control the color schemes
for image plots.  I received a couple of especially helpful replies.

>>From Mark Bravington
  graphsheet(num.image.colors = 2, num.image.shades = "64", 
    image.color.table = "255,0,0|255,255,0")
I happen to find it especially easy to interpret Mark's "shades of red"
using this color scheme.

A few people told me about options, color schemes from the Splus menu bar.
I initially had a hard time understanding how to implement their comments
until Ian Jonsen spelled out the specifics for me.  From the menu you can
use "Options  |  Graph Styles  |  Color"  and select from a list of possible
image color choices provided by the pull down menu.  If you don't like any
of these, you can create your own via  "Options  |  Color Schemes" and from
the image colors tab you can manually select colors and put them in the
User1 or User2 selection.  Then you can go back to the options\graph
styles\color menu and select User1 or User2 for your image color scheme.

Thanks to all who replied.  Since Ian's "detail" was especially helpful to
me, I'm adding below the full text of his reply for those who may be
interested in this issue.

Allen Humbolt
Koch Industries, Inc.
humbolta at kochind.com

>>From Ian Jonsen below:

In S-Plus 4.5 (win95) you can alter image colours by selecting Options \
Graph
Styles \ Colour

are
a few preset selections here that you can try, each one will use a different
set
of fill colours when image() is called. This might not work unless you open
a
new graphics device after you have selected an image colour scheme.

selecting:

Options \ Colour Schemes

select the Image Colours tab and go to the User 1 box. You can select the
number
of different colours you need and then choose the individual colours by
clicking
on the Edit colours button. I'm not sure what changing the "# of shades"
does.

You supplied d with zero values other than for self-distance, I gather.

aims. You could either drop one of the rows 8 and 12, or you could use
another form of MDS. Your message seems to suggest there are 9280
observations: if correct, you are going to find MDS slow and hard to

messages.subject: [S] Q: using aggregate and others....
messages.body_plain:
Dear S gurus,

I have been using the 'aggregate' function to split up a data set and
apply some function to each split. The nice things about using aggregate
are 
1) it is easy to use, 

2) it returns the result in a nice format 
   (columns for the split variables and the result). 
   It even handles the cases where not all sub-splits 
   are present in each split, which is nice. 

However, aggregate has several difficulties:

1) horribly slow for large datasets
2) can only work on a vector, not a matrix at a time
3) FUN can only produce a number, not a vector

The 'by' function addresses #2, but the output format of 'by' is awful. 

#3 would be nice for making several calculations on a each split. For
instance, being able to do the following : 
aggregate(data$a,list(lot=data$a,wafer=data$b),summary) 

would be nice. It would be even more useful in combination with #2
above, since then I could do more advanced calculations with a single
line. 

Of course, all of this is mostly to save the effort of writing loops and
such for each case. 

My questions to the group are as follows:

1) Has anyone developed replacements to aggregate that fix any/all of
the problems listed above?
2) If so, are these replacements available? 
3) If such things have not already been developed, what are suggestions
for avoiding problem #1 while achieving #2,3. i.e. are there
memory/efficiency tricks that I should know about before I start
fiddling with this?

I will summarize responses to the list.

Thank you very much.

regards,

messages.subject_clean: [S] Q: creating a new trellis panel
messages.body_plain:
Dear S group,

In the semiconductor industry, we have round wafers that are populated
with rectangular chips. In looking at the yield of each chip (#good/#),
it is useful to show a spatial map of all die and their yield. We
generated such a plotting routine and have been using it for a while. 

Recently, I realized that I could make it a trellis panel function,
which would allow me to do splits very easily in my plots. It seems that
contourplot does the correct set-up and allows the correct sort of
formulas, so this is what I figured out:

contour(shorts~x*y|lot, data, panel=panel.yieldmap)

The panel calculates the yield and makes the plot. 

Now, I then realized that this could be a more general function that
could plot TABLES of yield across different variables, with trellis
taking care of the looping and such for me. 

What I mean is something like this:

contour(shorts~temp*time|lot, data, panel=panel.yieldmap, as.table=T)

where as.table would tell the panel function to cast the x and y
variables as factors and plot a table instead of a graph (ie. don't use
the relative distances of the levels, but 1,2,3,...)

THe panel function works fine. However, the setup.2d.trellis function
tries to calculate the size of the panels and doesn't understand what I
am trying to do. As a result, I get garbage and errors from trellis
before even getting to my panel function. 

Now bwplot and some others allow factors in either the x or y axis, so I
tried looking into what they do. However, the heirarchy of functions is
pretty deep and I got lost. 

My question for you is this: how can I trick trellis into allowing
something like I have described?

Is there a better base function (not contourplot), or is there some
simple fix to the trellis code?

Any help with this will be very much appreciated!

I will summarize to the group.

regards,
jcd

ps. I am using Splus3.4 on Solaris.

messages.body_plain:
Dear you

I'm a student at the Swiss Federal Institut of technology, and I have a
serious issue with S-plus. I'm doing a study for optimizing the
replenishment of a big company during promotion periods. I would like to
get a model for forecasting the sales during these periods.
Basicly, I try to obtain a model giving the sale increase depending on
the abverage sales before the promotion, on the promotion duration, on
the retailer chanel, on the product category and on the promotion type.
I have 97 mesures. The factors are:
Factor1= average sales, split in 6 levels
Factor2= promotion duration, split in 5 levels
Factor3= retail channels, 3 levels
Factor4= product category, 3 levels
Factor5= promotion type, 6 levels\
F1= sale increase coefficient between avg sales and promotion sales
The total number of cell is the 1620, which makes my dataset highly
unbalanced.
I would like to know if the command AOV in S-plus handles 5 way
unbalanced AOV.
Because if I use 1,2,3 or 4 factors the liberty degrees are ok, but when
I add the 5th factor, the result of the analysis shows one degree less
than what should be the right value (lib.degree LD of Factor 5 = 4
(instead of 5))
Here is the input I did in S-plus

F1<- c(.... the 97 values of the increase coef)
Fact1<- c(... the 97 values of the first factor corresponding to the F1
values)
Fact2<- c(... same for 2nd factor)
Fact3<- c(...same)
Fact4<- c(...same)
Fact5<- c(...same)

Then I converted my factors into S-plus factor with the command
"factor".

Factor1<-factor(Fact1, levels=c(1,2,3,4,5,6))
Factor2<-factor(Fact2, levels=c(1,2,3,4,5))
Factor3<-factor(Fact3, levels=c(1,2,3))
Factor4<-factor(Fact4, levels=c(1,2,3))
Factor5<-factor(Fact5, levels=c(1,2,3,4,5))

Then I set the contrasts options to have the sum of the coefficient for
each factor to zero (command that someone indicated to me -  I use
S-plus only since the beginning of the week)

options(contrasts=c("contr.sum", "contr.sum"))

Then I do my analysis of variance, taking into account only the 2nd
level of interaction (more is not necessary)

analysis<-aov(F1~Factor1 + Factor2 + Factor3 + Factor4 + Factor5 +
Factor1:Factor2 + Factor1:Factor3 + Factor1:Factor4 + Factor1:Factor5 +
Factor2:Factor3 + etc...)

And here is the issue, when I display the summary of my analysis (i.e.
summary(analysis)) I see that on the fifth factor the LD is 4 instead of
5. The same happens if I only use a model without interactions. But if I
use the same model with 4 factor (example: skip Factor3) the LD of
Factor5 is again right (i.e. =5)

Another issue I noticed (if really this is an issue, if not, could you

messages.subject: Re: [S] Isotonic regression
messages.body_plain:
One simple method for least squares isotonic regression is using
non-negative least squares with an appropriately constructed design matrix.
The following function performs isotonic regression using the S-PLUS
function nnls.fit() for the non-negative least squares fitting. You can also
snag it from ftp://www.psych.uiuc.edu/pub/share/tjohnson/isoreg.txt.

isoreg <- function(x, y, weights = rep(1, length(x)), ties = F, ...)
{
# Purpose: isotonic regression of y on x. Returns fitted
#  values.
# Arguments: x is the regressor and y is the regressand.
#  Weights are optional. The ties option preserves ties
#  in x.
# Author: Tim R. Johnson (tjohnson at s.psych.uiuc.edu)
#
        if(ties) {
                m <- outer(rank(x), sort(unique(rank(x))), function(arg1,
arg2)
                arg1 >= arg2)
        }
        else {
                m <- outer(rank(rank(x) + runif(length(x))), 1:length(x),
function(arg1, arg2)
                arg1 >= arg2)
        }
        b <- nnls.fit(cbind(-1, m), y, weights = weights, ...)$coefficients
        as.vector(cbind(-1, m) %*% b)
}

messages.body_plain:
> From: Doug Moog <dbm3 at po.cwru.edu>
> For example, below I show a summary of an lm model.  Note that for the
> leading term, T.mean, Pr(>|t|) = 0.2042.   Then I call anova() on the same
> model, and get Pr(F) = 0.0000031457 for the same term.  Why such a
> difference?  Obviously I don't
> understand what at least one of these p-values represents.

The t-test is a test of the hypothesis that a coefficient is 0 in a
model containing all of the other variables.  The anova() results are
sequential, i.e. the first term is tested against a null model
containing no other terms.  (This is indicated by the phrase in the
header, "Terms added sequentially (first to last)".)  If T.mean is 
collinear with some of the other terms, it is likely to contribute much
less to model fit when other terms (including an interaction involving
T.mean itself) are already there, than it would as the only term in the
model.

messages.subject: [S] cross-over designs & censored observations
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to analyze several data sets from cross-over experiments that
have (Type I) censored data. I am using the methods of Wei, Lin & Weissfeld
(1989; "Regression analysis of multivariate incomplete failure time data by
modeling marginal distributions", JASA, '89, 84: 1065-1073), which I fit
using the cluster option with coxph.  However, there are a couple of
"peculiarities" in these data, and I would appreciate your feedback.

1. My sample sizes are small (10 to 30 individuals; each individual
observed 2 to 4 times; two response variables measured at each observation
time; each individual is subject to two treatments --see below).  Does any
one now about the performance of WLW's method with these sample sizes?

2. The data come from cross-over desings.  Suppose the design with
sequences ABBA/BAAB:  here about half of the animals receive treatment A,
then B, then B, then A; and the other half the other sequence. For each
animal, at each of the 4 times, I measure two response variables (e.g., Y1,
Y2, times until the animal performs behaviors 1 and 2 respectively).  In
other words, I have repeated multivariate observations for each individual.

My main interest is to test the hypotheses of no treatment effects (A vs.
B)  a multiv. hypoth., as I have two response vars]; but my models also
need to include period, sequnce, and carry-over.  I think that the test of
no treatment  effect is done testing  Ho: betaY1 = betaY2 = 0 (where beta
is the treatment-specific regression parameter), with the quadratic form W
(p. 1066 of WLW).

To do this in SPlus I basically follow p. 20-35 and 20-36 of SPlus manual
(v. 3.3 for Windows); [similar information can be found in document
survival4.doc available from statlib] with a few additions

>mult.cox<-coxph(Surv(Time,Status)~ (Sequence+Period+ Tretament +
Carryover) * strata(TypeofResponse) + cluster   (ID),data=exp3)  # i.e., the
type of response variable is entered as a stratum; 

> Trt<-c(3,7) #where coefficients for treatment are in mult.cox
> cmat<-diag(2);cmat[,1]<-1 #obtain contrast matrix
> nu<-cmat%*%mult.cox$coef[Trt] #the vector nu, as in p. 1066 of Wei et al.
(WLW).
> wvar<-cmat%*%mult.cox$var[Trt,Trt]%*%t(cmat)  #variance matrix
> W<-t(nu)%*%solve(wvar)%*%nu #obtaining the quadr. form W (p. 1066); this
is the one used to test the multiv. hypoth      that there is no treatment 
effect
> 1-pchisq(W,length(nu)) # chi-square test of multiv. hypoth.

messages.subject: [S] Inside summary -- vectorization
messages.body_plain:
First, thanks go to Robert Garret for providing the history of this
topic on S-news; to Brian Ripley for outlining an efficient algorithm;
to Peter Perkins for his program "region.in" (which was the first
mentioned in
Garret's history); to John Wallace for providing a copy of the same
under the title "region.inside"; and to Franz Mueter, for pointing to the 
"points.in.poly" function, which is part of the Spatial module,
and is written directly in C.

Peter Perkins program, given below, is based on centering the extreme
points around each test point and checking if the sum of radians from the
test
point to successive extreme points is close to 2*pi.

Brian Ripley's suggestion:

 A convex polygon is defined by r enclosing half-planes a + bx + cy >= 0.
So find them (you need the extreme points in order, which I think chull
gives, then the lines pass through successive pairs) and make a matrix A
with columns a b c. The test is then 

((cbind(1, X) %*% t(A) < 0) %*% rep(1, r)) == 0

which gives a vector with T for inside, F for outside.

 This seems like a good idea, so I implemented a version of it. I was
too lazy to check which side of each half-plane the hull was was on,
so I just computed the average m of the extreme points (which is 
guaranteed to be inside the region) and checked that each test point
was on the same side of all the boundary lines as m. This function
"Inside" is given below, right after "region.in".

 As far as efficiency, I sampled 10,000 points at random from the unit
square and tested if they were in the convex quadrilateral defined by
> hull
     [,1] [,2] 
[1,]  0.0  0.0
[2,]  0.2  0.4
[3,]  0.6  1.0
[4,]  1.0  0.0

The two procedures worked about equally well:

> unix.time(region.in(testpts,rbind(hull,c(0,0))))
[1] 2.3399963 0.1100001 5.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000
> unix.time(Inside(testpts,hull))
[1] 2.18999481 0.03000021 3.00000000 0.00000000 0.00000000

Both were much faster than my initial crude attempt:
>unix.time(apply(testpts,1,inside,h=hull))
[1] 167.30   0.77 343.00   0.00   0.00
where 
inside _ function(pt,hull) min(chull(rbind(pt,h)))>1

Thanks to all for your patience and information -- 
 I guess those who repeat history are compelled to learn from it!

region.in <- function(test, vertices)
{
# determine whether test points are inside a simply closed polygon.
# this routine uses EUCLIDEAN geometry, not SPHERICAL.
#
# test:         matrix (or 2-vector) of test points
# vertices:     matrix of polygon vertices, last vertex same as first
#
# col1 = x-coords, col2 = y-coords
#
       n <- nrow(vertices) - 1
       if(!is.matrix(test)) test <- matrix(test, nrow = 1, byrow = T)  #
#
# translate to coords centered at each test point
       x <-  - outer(test[, 1], vertices[1:n, 1], "-")
       y <-  - outer(test[, 2], vertices[1:n, 2], "-") #
#
# tan(theta) = (v1 x v2) / (v1 * v2)
       i2 <- c(2:n, 1)
       theta <- atan(x * y[, i2] - y * x[, i2], x * x[, i2] + y * y[,
i2])     #
#
# sum angles about each test point
       theta <- abs(theta %*% rep(1, n))
       ifelse(abs(theta - 2 * pi) < 1e-06, T, F)
}

____________________________________________________________
                
Inside _ function(pts,h=hull){
#
# Input:
#    pts -- (n x 2) matrix of test points
#      h -- ([k+1] x 2) matrix of (ordered) vertices,
#                 [with last row = first row]
# Output:
#     (n x 1) logical vector indicating inclusion of tests points
#           in the convex polygon formed by h 
#
n _ nrow(pts)
k _ nrow(h)-1
if (!all(h[1,]==h[k+1,])) {
    h_ rbind(h,h[1,])
    k _ k+1}
#
# compute slopes and intercepts of boundary lines
#
b _ diff(h[,2])/diff(h[,1])
a _ diag(h[1:k,] %*%t(cbind(-b,1)))
#
#   compute centroid and its residuals from boundary lines
#
m _ rep(1/k,k) %*%  h[1:k,]
r0 _  m[2] - (a + b* m[1])
#
#  compute residuals of test points from boundary lines
#
r _ outer(pts[,2],rep(1,k)) - outer(pts[,1],b) - outer(rep(1,n),a)
signs _ (r %*% diag(r0)) > 0
ans _  as.vector(signs %*% rep(1,k) == k)
ans}

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
    I am looking for some info/software for bump hunting. Specifically I
am working with some data from High Energy Physics that has some
suspicious bumps that may or may not correspond to a particle decay and
I would like to investigate this further. The currently used method in
HEP is to fit a parametric curve to the data (usually via maximum
likelihood) and thereby to get an estimate (and its error) for the
number of events in the bump. If that number is several standard
deviations above 0 (usually somewhat more than 3 sd are required) than
they start to believe that the bump is real. I am looking for a
nonparametric alternative to this method.
In addition there is often some prior info from the theory on whether or
not there might be a bump in this area, either because other experiments
have already seen some evidence for it or maybe because the theory sort
of predicts a bump there. How can I incorporate this type of info in the
analysis? I guess this is asking for a Bayesian approach. Unfortunately
I am not very good at Bayesian analysis, so if somebody can point me to
a paper that discusses "Bayesian bump hunting", I would be very
grateful.

Wolfgang

one natural alternative is to fit a mixture distribution.  as I 
understand the problem you have several peaks in a histogram, and
want to fit something other than a single parametric distribution.
if you think of each bump as a sample from its own distribution,
the problem is to estimate the mixing probabilities (the proportion
in each bump) and the parameters of that distribution.

take a look at Titterington, Smith, and Makov's book
"Statistical Analysis of Finite Mixture Distributions"
They also at least briefly discuss bayesian methods, which
might indeed be appropriate here.  There is also a group
at the University of Washington (Adrain Raftery is the name that
leaps to mind) working on related problems.

> deviations above 0 (usually somewhat more than 3 sd are required) than
> they start to believe that the bump is real. I am looking for a
> nonparametric alternative to this method.

Two nonparametric approaches are Silverman's bandwidth test and the
excess mass test.  Silverman's test uses as a test statistic the
minimum bandwidth for which a kernel density estimate (with normal
kernel) is unimodal.  The excess mass test is somewhat more difficult
to explain in one sentence, but seems to be equivalent to Hartigan and
Hartigan's DIP test.  To achieve reasonable power, these tests need to
be calibrated.  Ming Yen Cheng and Peter Hall do this for the excess
mass test in the JRSS-B paper cited below.  Matthew York, a student of
Peter Hall, has done the same for Silverman's test in his thesis, but
I don't believe that this has been published yet.

I don't know what sort of software is available publically, although
I'm think I've seen something out there for the DIP test.

Brett Presnell

messages.subject: [S] Announcing ESS 5.1.2
messages.body_plain:
Annoucing the release of ESS-5.1.2 (Emacs Speaks Statistics).
-------------------------------------------------------------

(New: improvements to SAS support,
      Splus 5 support, 
      Splus 4.5 under Microsoft Windows support)

ESS is an Emacs package which provides a standard interface between
statistical programs and statistical processes.  It is intended to
provide assistance for interactive statistical programming and data
analysis, and was is based on and extends the capabilities of S-mode.
The code is freely available but is not in the public domain.  It is
distributed under the GNU GPL.  Please read the file COPYING for more
information about the license.

ESS grew out of the desire to extend S-mode-4.8.  The current set of
developers desired support for:
- XEmacs
- R
- S4
- Microsoft Windows

In addition, with new modes being developed for R, Stata, and SAS, it
was felt a unifying interface and framework for the user interface,
would benefit both the user and the developer, by helping both groups
conform to standard Emacs usage.  The end result is an increase in
efficiency for statistical programming and data analysis, over the
usual tools.

We are grateful to David M. Smith , the previous developer (for S-mode
3.x and 4.x), as well as to the initial developers of S-mode, Doug
Bates, Ed Kademan and Frank Ritter.

And to help remove any further confusion:

        The name is __ESS__.  Not ESS-mode.

Thank you :-).

0.5. NEW FEATURES IN THIS RELEASE!
----------------------------------

Beginning with ESS 5.1.2 we are able to use inferior iESS mode to
communicate directly with a running S-Plus 4.x process using the
Microsoft DDE protocol.  We use the familiar (from Unix ESS) C-c C-n
and related key sequences to send lines from the S-mode file to the
inferior S process.  We continue to edit S input files in ESS[S] mode
and transcripts of previous S sessions in ESS Transcript mode.  All
three modes know the S language, syntax, and indentation patterns and
provide the syntactic highlighting that eases the programming tasks.

1. FEATURES
-----------

Languages Supported (or planned for support)

- S dialects: S 3/4, S-PLUS 3.x/4.x/5.x, and R
- LispStat dialects: XLispStat (planned: ViSta)
- SAS
- (planned: Stata)
- (planned: SPSS dialects (SPSS, PSPP))

Editing source code (S, LispStat, SAS)

- Syntactic indentation and highlighting of source code
- Evaluations of subsets of code in different processes (one at a
  time)
- Loading and error-checking of code
- Source code revision maintenance
- limited interaction with Noweb, for literate statistical
  programming.

Interacting with the process (S, LispStat, SAS)

- Command-line editing
- Searchable Command history
- Command-line completion of S object names and file names
- Quick access to object lists and search lists
- Transcript recording
- Interface to the help system

Transcript manipulation (S3, S+3, S+4, S4, S+5, R, XLispStat)

- Recording and saving transcript files
- Manipulating and editing saved transcripts
- Re-evaluating commands from transcript files

2. STABILITY
------------

Version 5.1.2 is meant as a new feature release, with some bug fixes
from ESS 5.0.  We consider it BETA-software.  In particular, 

3. REQUIREMENTS
---------------

ESS version 5.2 requires Emacs version 19.29, XEmacs version 19.14, or
later version.  ESS is supposed to work with any version of S, S-PLUS,
R, SAS, or XLispStat.

It has been most thoroughly tested with:

        S-PLUS 3.3 and 3.4, S4, R 0.49 and 0.50, XLispStat 3.50, and
        SAS on (when available) SunOS, Solaris, SGI, and Linux (Unix)
        systems;

        Emacs 19.29, 19.34, XEmacs 19.16, XEmacs 20.4.

        Emacs 19.28 with SAS (with additional modifications)

        NTEmacs 20.2.1 with S-PLUS 4.5.

It may need some work with other configurations.  We have included
configuration suggestions for emacs 19.28 and SAS in Doc/README-19.28.

Suggestions and information about attempts to port to
Microsoft-developed operating systems are encouraged.  In particular,
it is an open question whether or not it can be implemented for
XLispStat, ViSta, R, S-PLUS 4.0, Stata, and SAS under a Microsoft
environment using NTEmacs (or the version of XEmacs for Microsoft
Windows NT currently under development).  In particular, the
developers need information on how to redirect the listener and
command-line output and input for the above statistical programs.

4. GETTING THE LATEST VERSION
-----------------------------

The latest versions of ESS are always available by WWW from:

        http://franz.stat.wisc.edu/pub/ESS/
        ftp://franz.stat.wisc.edu/pub/ESS/

You can download the current version of the README there, as well.

The HTML version of the documentation can be found at:

        http://stat.ethz.ch/ESS/

The most recent developers release of ESS can be obtained via
anonymous CVS by...  (NEED TO ADD INFORMATION!)

5. THE ESS MAILING LIST
--------------------------

There is a mailing list for discussions and announcements relating to
ESS.  Join the list by sending an e-mail with "subscribe ess-help"
(or "help") in the body to ess-help-request at stat.math.ethz.ch;
contributions to the list may be mailed to ess-help at stat.math.ethz.ch.
Rest assured, this is a fairly low-volume mailing list.

The purposes of the mailing list include

- helping users of ESS to get along with it.
- discussing aspects of using ESS for GNU Emacs and XEmacs.
- suggestions for improvements.
- announcements of new [beta] releases of ESS.
- posting small patches to ESS.

messages.subject: RE: [S] bump hunting
messages.body_plain:
Wolfgang:
        If it would be of interest to you, I wrote a thesis on bump hunting
in regression recently. The copy of it is on the web:
http://hajek.stat.ubc.ca/~nancy/pubs.html

In brief, my method works in the regression context with one regressor.
Also, I can look for bumps in the derivatives of regression functions. My
idea is based on Silverman's bandwidth test (1981) for kernel density
estimates, and its extension by Bowman et.al. (1998) to monotonicity testing
in regression context.

References:
Silverman, B. W. (1981) "Using Kernel Density Estimates to Investigate
Multimodality" JRSS-B, 43, pp. 97-99
Bowman, A.W., Jones, M.C., and Gijbels, I. (1998) "Testing Monotonicity of
Regression", Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 7, pp.
489-500

I developed the code in Splus for the bump hunting using smoothing splines
and kernel methods. I was not able to completely document the code yet, but
I can provide it to you with partial documentation and further explanation,
if you'd need any.

Jarek

messages.subject: Re: [S] ksmooth(),density(), and Haerdle
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 11 Feb 1999, Thomas J. Richards wrote:

This is easy: for kde the bandwidth is the standard deviation: for 
density it is 4x the standard deviation. Compare

> hb<-kde(data=buffalo$b,kernel=6, h=8, points=100)
> db<-density(x=buffalo$b,n=100,width=32,cut=1,window="gaussian")

Be aware that kde as in Haerdle's book is extraordinarily slow, and the kde
in the version of library haerdle in statlib is re-written by me: the
original is kde.old and is even slower than ksmooth.

You could try reading the help pages!  For density:

width:    width of the window.  The default is  the  width  of  a
       histogram   bar  which  is  determined  by  log(length(x),
       base=2) + 1 bars to cover the range of  x.   The  standard
       error  of  a  Gaussian  window  is width/4.

(One wonders about the author's grasp of Statistics 101.)

For ksmooth 

bandwidth:     the kernel  bandwidth  smoothing  parameter.   All
       kernels are scaled so the upper and lower quartiles of the
       kernel (viewed as a probability density) are +/- 0.25 when
       bandwidth  is 1.

which is not simply related to the others. A bandwidth of 21.5 seems a 
good match.  The quartiles of a standard normal are at +/-0.674, so the 
formula gives 8 *(0.674/0.25) = 21.57.

I think bkde in Matt Wand's library KernSmooth is preferable to any of 
these.  Its bandwidth agrees with that of density.

> Techniques, code from StatLib.  I can't figure out what Splus 4.5

messages.subject_clean: [S] names of functions in a list?
messages.body_plain:
From: Tim Smith <tsmith at whsun1.wh.whoi.edu>

> What I'd like to be able to do, however, is to automatically 
> construct the names of the functions passed in list(min,mean,max),
> rather than having to use the syntax min=min.  

That list does not contain the function names, only the function
bodies. However,

nlist <- function(...)
{
   nm <- unlist(as.list(match.call())[-1])
   dots <- list(...)
   names(dots) <- nm
   dots
}
tapply(x, y, FUN=nlist(min,mean,max)[[2]])

will do what you want.  So will

tapply(x, y, FUN=c("min", "mean", "max")[2])

since tapply can be used with function names too.

[Just don't ask why nlist works: demonstrating how to manipulate ... 
is a rite of passage.]

messages.subject: [S] Bug in smooth.spline
messages.body_plain:
We recently discovered a small bug in the function smooth.spline;
the bug may be innocent when smooth.spline is used interactively,
but not when (as in our case) the output of smooth.spline is used
directly as input for other computations.

According to the documentation for smooth.spline, there may be ties 
in the x argument, as long as there are at least ten distinct 
x values.  However, we found that near-ties among the smallest x 
values can cause trouble, as in this case (here we use Version 3.4 
Release 1 for Sun SPARC, SunOS 5.3; however the same bug occured
on a PC with Splus 4.5):

> x
 [1] -1.40461 -1.40460 -1.40459 -1.27158 -1.23411
 [6] -1.12842 -1.12448 -1.12033 -0.91474 -0.87535
[11] -0.84843 -0.65776 -0.63444 -0.46434 -0.28305
[16] -0.25552 -0.24259 -0.22592 -0.14116 -0.05622
> y
 [1]  0.69315  0.40547  2.00000  0.24816  1.47703
 [6]  1.94555  0.68579 -0.02887  1.31648  0.75097
[11]  1.04324  0.59080  0.42554  0.37129  0.03544
[16] -1.41142 -0.86375 -1.42216  0.56644 -0.93516
> smooth.spline(x, y, df=4)$df
[1] 14.62833

Plotting the fitted spline confirms that the result
is anything but smooth.  Note that if we round the
x values to four decimals, thus making the three
first x values identical, the problem disappears:

> smooth.spline(round(x,4), round(y,4), df=4)$df
[1] 4.004533

Using s() in gam can lead to similar problems.

messages.body_plain:
>>>>> "Marc" == Marc Feldesman <feldesmanm at pdx.edu> writes:

    Marc> I have need to compute a Mahanobis distance matrix
    Marc> between group centroids of 28 different groups.
    Marc> (Because the analysis will need to be related to a
    Marc> discriminant analysis of the identical data, and can be
    Marc> derived from same, I need to derive the distances from
    Marc> the pooled within groups covariance matrix).  I'm not
    Marc> interested in the distances between individuals within
    Marc> a group and the group centroid, or distances between
    Marc> individuals in one group and the centroids of another
    Marc> group.  All of this information is useful, but not
    Marc> germane to the analysis (and display of results) I want
    Marc> to perform.

    Marc> The mahalanobis function does not seem to do what I
    Marc> need.  Can some one point me to a routine that gives
    Marc> the necessary information or already does this type of
    Marc> calculation.  I can roll my own if necessary (I think),
    Marc> but I'd rather not reinvent the wheel if there exists a
    Marc> well-tested routine already out there to do the same
    Marc> thing.

I think all you need do is use mahalanobis() within apply().
Here is a mock-up example:

> X <- matrix(rnorm(28*10*4), 28*10, 4)
> f <- factor(rep(1:28, 10))

> fm <- aov(X ~ f-1)  # using `-1' here makes the next line work
> B <- coef(fm)       # matrix of group means 

> V <- crossprod(resid(fm))/(28*9)  # `within' variance matrix
 
> DM <- apply(B, 1, function(x) mahalanobis(B, x, V))

Now DM is the (symmetric) matrix of Mahalanobis distances between
group means relative to the within-group variance matrix estimate.

Notes:

1. This actually does twice the work needed since it computes
   both halves of the symmetric distance matrix, but I can't see
   any snazzy way of avoiding that.... (challenge?)

2. If you were doing the last step within a function you may need
   to use the `extra arguments' dodge with apply() to take care
   of visibility issues:

DM <- apply(B, 1, function(x, B, V) mahalanobis(B, x, V), B=B, V=V)

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: [S] Re: your mail
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 16 Feb 1999, Peter So wrote:

> Is S-Plus capable to do reml analysis in field and agricultural 
> experiments such as Genstat does?

S is a general programming language, so it is certainly capable of this,
whatever `reml analysis' is meant.  Now as I understand it REML is
residual/reduced/restricted maximum likelihood, and so a method of
estimation: you also need a model to estimate for an analysis. And what is
the difference between field and agricultural experiments? I always
thought field trials were a special case of agricultural experiments.

The classical analysis of field trials would be done by the aov function in
S using an Error term, and although not usually expressed that way gives a
REML analysis. (For balanced designs the only issues are how you estimate
the variance components: for the fixed effects all reasonable methods of
estimation agree. It seems that REML was developed to extend the classical
methods to unbalanced problems.)

Two other ways to give a REML analysis in existing S software are functions
varcomp and lme, both of which can consider unbalanced designs. There is an
enhanced version of lme in beta release at

        http://nlme.stat.wisc.edu/Beta

with which it is easier to analyse multistratum experiments.

All of these methods are considered in Venables & Ripley (1997, chapter
10), even illustrated on an agricultural field trial.  And (my main reason
for posting a reply) the on-line statistical complements now have a chapter
showing how to use the latest lme on the examples in the book.

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 16 Feb 1999, Peter So wrote:

> Is S-Plus capable to do reml analysis in field and agricultural
> experiments such as Genstat does?

If all you want is estimates of the variance components the answer here is
yes. For some reason some packages seem to think this is enough.

If you want tables of mean effects (BLUEs for fixed effects and BLUPs for
random effects) and standard errors of differences for these means as
Genstat REML (based on the original REML program from the Scottish
Agricultural Service) gives automatically, then the answer is no. The Splus
aov() and model.tables() functions with give the  required information but
only for balanced designs.
Genstat is the only package I know of where mean effects and standard
errors are readily available for balanced and unbalanced multistratum
experimental designs.

To quote from Venables and Ripley , Modern applied statistics with Splus
p302: "A better appreciation of the results of the experiment comes from
looking at the estimated marginal means. Tables of means are only available
for balanced designs and the standard errors calculated are for differences
of means" .

Actually tables of 'means' are available from Splus model.tables() for
unbalanced designs (but these are not the mean effects, and standard errors
of differences require further calculations using se.contrast() ) . The
help file for model.tables() does not specify only balanced designs.

It is possible with further computation to calculate mean effects and
standard errors of differences using the fitted model object from
varcomp(). The example below is an unbalanced dataset based on 50 randomly
chosen points from the 'oats' example shown on page 303 of V&R. Note how
the mean effects tables are closer to the results of the analysis of the
full balanced data set than the means from model.tables().  eg for Nitrogen
0.4cwt the estimate is 114.2 from the full data set, the mean effect is 114
and the value from model.tables() is 105.7 .

Provisos: my model.tables function is designed for factors (not covariates)
and varcomp() will baulk if the model matrix is singular, which it
sometimes is in analysis of variance type models.

Rod Ball

Dr Roderick D. Ball                                Ph 64-7-3475899
Statistician,                 Fx 64-7-3479380
New Zealand Forest Research Institute    email: ballr at fri.cri.nz
P.B. 3020, Rotorua, New Zealand

obviously this was a simple question. Thanks to all who replied.
The simplest solution is to use the levels subcommand for the factor
function, instead of using the cut function.

my.factor <- factor(my.continous, levels=1:max(my.continous))

automatically.

You state that

    I tried SAS proc CATMOD, but this allows only to a limited degree

I presume that you declared the interval scaled predictors in the DIRECT

Matthew Zack

From: "Brian P. Flaherty" <bxf4 at psu.edu>

Matthias,
        I asked the very same question last year. The easiest thing I found was 
to
use the multinom() command in Ripley's nnet library (available at Statlib

Brian Flaherty

If you install the Venables and Ripley libraries (MASS, spatial,
treefix, nnet, class) in the nnet library there is a function
multinomial() that does precisely what you want.  You call it
like an ordinary model fitting function:

        library(nnet)
        fm <- multinomial(H ~ x1 + x2 + ...., data = Stuttgart)

assigned to and x1, x2 .... are the predictors, with no
restrictions on them.  There are the usual method functions for
doing things with the fitted model object, too, including predict().

though.  A couple of hundred patients should be fine, but a

messages.subject: Re: [S] cox proportional models
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 23 Feb 1999, Chung-chi Chang wrote:

> I tried to do the estimation from cox proportional hazards models 
> by specifying the baseline intensity follows "Weibull" forms.
> I don't see "coxph" codes in s-plus can do that, can't it? Or I have 
> to use "survreg" to find the scale parameter of the Weibull on 
> baseline intensity function?

The Cox proportional hazards model (note `Cox' is capitalized: he is a
living person) assumes a non-parametric baseline hazard. The Weibull model
is also a proportional hazard model and can be fitted by survreg, but you
will need to transform the coefficients to PH form: see Venables & Ripley
for worked examples. The coefficients will be different when you assume
a Weibull or non-parametric baseline hazard.

messages.subject: [S] Idiosyncracy in GAM function
messages.body_plain:
I have just discovered an interesting feature of the gam function. In
fitting complex time series data using quasi-likelihood, I have found that
the final results of the fit depend on the order of the covariates. For
example, the model

log(y) = a + lo(day,span=0.05) + lo(year) + lo(x) 

will give slightly different estimates of the dispersion parameter,
residual deviances, residual degrees of freedom, standard errors and the
like than a model, say,

log(y) = a + lo(year) + lo(x) + lo(day,span=0.05). 
 
The differences all occur in the fifth decimal place, so that the effects 
are extremely minor, but nevertheless disconcerting.

I'm curious to know whether any one else has run into this and whether 
there is a simple explanation. 

Mark Goldberg,PhD

messages.subject: Re: [S] Warning message when rbinding
messages.body_plain:
This is a factor problem, if a column in the first data frame does not
have all the levels of the matching column in a subsequent data frame
then this error occurs.

I have also been struggling with this problem recently.  As luck would
have it, just today, I have found a solution.  (Note, another
approach would be to turn off the 'auto convert to factor' of the data
frames, as some people have done.)

The following function only handles two data frames at a time, but it
should solve your problem. 

rbind.df <- function(df1, df2)
{
#
#   DATE WRITTEN:  February 1999 
#   AUTHOR:  John R. Wallace (jrw at fish.washington.edu)
#
# 'which.fac' is needed to prevent other classes from being affected
# 
        which.fac <- (1:ncol(df1))[unlist(lapply(df1, is.factor))]
        out <- rbind(data.frame(lapply(df1, function(x)
        {
                if(is.factor(x))
                        I(as.character(x))
                else x
        }
        )), data.frame(lapply(df2, function(x)
        {
                if(is.factor(x))
                        I(as.character(x))
                else x
        }
        )))
        out[, which.fac] <- data.frame(lapply(out[, which.fac], 
                function(x)
        {
                class(x) <- NULL
                x
        }
        ))
        out
}

On Tue, 23 Feb 1999, Mark Goldberg (mark at polair.epi.mcgill.ca) wrote:

> 
> I have just discovered an interesting feature of the gam function. In
> fitting complex time series data using quasi-likelihood, I have found that
> the final results of the fit depend on the order of the covariates. For
> example, the model
> 
> log(y) = a + lo(day,span=0.05) + lo(year) + lo(x) 
> 
> will give slightly different estimates of the dispersion parameter,
> residual deviances, residual degrees of freedom, standard errors and the
> like than a model, say,
> 
> log(y) = a + lo(year) + lo(x) + lo(day,span=0.05). 
>  
> The differences all occur in the fifth decimal place, so that the effects 
> are extremely minor, but nevertheless disconcerting.
> 
> I'm curious to know whether any one else has run into this and whether 
> there is a simple explanation. 

Try changing the convergence criteria in gam.control. Like glm, gam has
rather loose convergence default criteria: in both cases the lack of
convergence is rarely important.

More seriously, there is a priori no reason why a gam model need have a
single solution, and we have seen examples where equivalent models using
s() that converge to different solutions (with different
(quasi-)likelihoods).  When using lo() it is even unclear what problem a
gam is solving.

Splus users,

I recently posted the following question:

>I am looking for an Splus function which would estimate the parameters
>of a dirichlet-multinomial mixture (the multicategory analogue of

>

I received the following responses from ....

Dean Billheimer
----------------

I don't have an S-plus function that directly estimates the
Dirichlet-multinomial parameters.  Several years ago I wrote some Splus
code to perform this feat, and I don't think there was too much involved
(I'm afraid the code fell by the way-side.)  Mosimann (1962, I think)
published a paper in Biometrika that provides expressions for the maximum
likelihood estimators for the parameters.  These can be solved numerically
with nlmin() or nlminb().  As I recall, the only (relatively) tricky part
was to re-parameterize so that the minizer uses only positive values for
the parameter estimates (like exp(x)).  (This may have been before
nlminb() was available.)

Thomas Yee
-----------

I think my VGAM software (http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/yee/vgam)
should be able to handle it, provided somebody writes a family function
for it. 

Dave Fournier also replied that he has some software that could do the job.
-------------

Thanks for these responses!
Melanie Wigg

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 25 Feb 1999, Hannoever wrote:

> I fear this might be an FAQ, but is there a function to plot the hazard
> function for a Kaplan Meier survival function?

Not really, as there is not a hazard function. The KM _estimate_ of the
survivor function is a step function: only (a.e) differentiable survival
distributions have hazard functions you could plot.

If you can be more precise we may be able to help: there are ways to
estimate hazard functions from data (see Chapter 12 of the V&R2 Statistical
Complements), and you can do cumulative hazard plots.

pad.string <- function(x, len = max(nchar(x)), padchar = " ", right = T){
  ## pads x to the right (default) or left with padchar to desired length

    stop("nchar(padchar) != 1")
  template <- paste(rep(padchar, len), collapse = "")
  if(right)
    xpad <- paste(substring(template, 1 + nchar(x)), x, sep = "")
  else  
    xpad <- paste(x, substring(template, 1 + nchar(x)), sep = "")
  attributes(xpad) <- attributes(x)
  xpad

messages.subject: [S] Tests for multivariate NON-normality?
messages.body_plain:
A recent query asked about tests for multivariate normality.  It has long
seemed to me that the term "tests for normality" (even for univariate ones)
is a misleading name since they are really tests for NON-normality, and as I
understand matters, most have only low power to find that (unless sample
size
is very large).

As with any significance test, failure to reject the null hypothesis does
not provide evidence FOR that hypothesis.  In this application, failing to
demonstrate non-normality does not (or at least should not) leave you at all
confident that you *have* normality.  If normality is important for some
reason, then in my view, one should use normal probability plots, empirical
density plots, and possibly estimates of skewness and kurtosis, along with
judgment, to decide whether the data at hand are "normal enough" or not.

I suggest that anyone using this kind of test should generate 1000 or so
datasets (of sample size comparable to their own) with normality that is
marginally unacceptable in the way suspected for one's data.  Then apply the
proposed test to those datasets, and check whether it performs adequately.

Note that "tests for homogeneity of variance" are (il)logically similar
---they are really tests for non-homogeneity, and a non-significant result
provides little evidence that "all is well."   Isn't the ratio of the
largest
to the smallest variance more relevant than a p value if skedasticity is at
issue?

Dave Parkhurst

town in the snowstorm, then you know that it *can* travel through snow.  If

messages.body_plain:
I hesitate to engage in this discussion, as it is rapidly degenerating into
the usual sort of blather when people get sloppy. So briefly:

1. NO data *are* normal. Normality is a mathematical entity, not a property
of data. One may use a normal distribution as an empirical model that
approximates data. One may also use any of 562 other distributions that may
do equally well. As George Box remarked: "All models are wrong, but some are
useful."

2. Given enough real data, any test of normality will reject (a
meta-theorem?); this does not necessarily mean that a normal model does not
usefully characterize the data.

3. Given little enough data, any test of normality will fail to reject; this
does not necessarily mean that a normal model will usefully characterize the
data.

4. The above 2 points are why power/sample size (or versions thereof like OC
curves) must be considered in applying N-P theory.

5. If the above 3 points bother you, become a Bayesian.

on the Biostatistics web site
        http://www.mayo.edu/hsr/biostat.html
in the software section.  Some useful documentation is also found in my
own page under the Lead statistician section.

   There are dozens of changes with respect to "survival4".  Most of these
have already been incorporated into Splus; for these the release acts as
the ultimate documentation, i.e., source code.  Major changes that are not
yet part of the Splus release are

   - penalized Cox models.  These include smoothing splines, frailty 
(random effects) and ridge regression as special cases.  User written
penalty functions are supported, so many more possibilities exist.
   - major rewrite of the parametric survival function survreg().  This
allows for penalized models (same extensions as coxph), user specified
distributions, a larger number of residuals and predicted values options,

errors that people have complained of, justifiably, for several years.

subscripting, e.g.  fit <- survfit(...); plot(fit[1:2],...); lines(fit[3],...)

Hello S+ Users,

Thanks to all who responded to my posting.  All recommended the format()
function.  I knew there had to be an easy way to pad with 0's.

Here is an example from Sam Buttrey:

> format (c(5, 0.62))
[1] "5.00" "0.62"

If you want to force everything to have three digits after the decimal,
use the nsmall= option:

> format (c(5, 0.62), nsmall = 3)
[1] "5.000" "0.620"
